full_judgment:
2. Opposite Party No. 1 Gageswar Nath filed a petition of complaint before the Upazila Magistrate, Patuakhali on 12.3.87 against one Nazrul Islam and Ismail alleging that they being armed with weapons kidnapped his daughter, the petitioner, with her valuable ornaments against her will with an evil motive from the bank of the tank on 9.3.87. The learned Magistrate took cognizance of the case under sections 366/109/379 of the Penal Code and issued warrant of arrest against the said two accused persons. The learned Magistrate also issued search warrant for the present petitioner who appeared before the court on 19.3.87 and she was ordered to be kept in judicial custody till her age was ascertained. 

 3. The petitioner was examined by a doctor who submitted a report in court that the age of the petitioner was bet ween 16-17 years on 2004.87. The opposite party No. 1, father of the petitioner filed an application before the learned Magistrate praying for giving the petitioner in his custody. The petitioner also filed an application on the same day praying for allowing her to go on her own bail alleging that she was aged 20 years and that she at her own will embraced Islam in Poush, 1390 BS and had taken Muslim name as Fatema Begum and married accused Nurul Islam and that the accused did not forcibly kidnap her. She swore an affidavit in support of those facts. The learned Magistrate allowed the father of the petitioner to take her in custody. 

 12. The learned Magistrate, therefore, has no jurisdiction to kept the petitioner in custody or to deliver her to the custody of her father. In this connection a reference may be made to the case of Jahanara Begum alias Jotsna Rani Shaha Vs. The State and another reported in 15 DLR 148 wherein a Division Bench of the High Court held that in a case to which section 100 of the Criminal Procedure Code is applicable, where a person brought before the Court is aged 16 years or over the will of such person, when the question before the Court is whether she (or he) should be detained or allowed to go from court's custody, must be allowed to prevail. The position of such a person is, at the most, that of a witness and therefore not being an accused she or he cannot be detained against her (or his) will. In the case of Ananda Mohan Banerjee Vs. State allas ors reported in 35 DLR 315 a Division Bench of this court held "…………….The victim girl who is above the age of 16 years as of to-day cannot be detained in custody against her will, as such the petitioner Ananda Mohan Banerjee is not entitled to the custody of the victim girl, as prayed for by him in the Rule and the victim girl is free to go wherever she likes." 

 13. Now the question is whether this Court will interfere with the order passed by the learned Sessions Judge in exercise of his power under section 439A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The present application has been filed under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure which is independent of section 439 of the same Code. Mr. Sobhan submits that although the application has been filed as one under section 561A CrPC it is in effect a second revisional application which is barred. In support of his contention he referred to the case of Nader Ali Shaikh Vs. The State all others reported in BCR 1984 (AD) 87 wherein the Appellate Division held "Section 561A may be invoked only for the specific purposes set out in this section and the High Court Division may in appropriate cases exercise its extraordinary power under this section to prevent the abuse of the process of the Court or to meet ends of justice. Provision of this section cannot be invoked by a person after becoming unsuccessful in an incompetent application for revision which is barred by law." So, in the case cited the exercise of power by this Court under section 561A has not been held to be totally barred against an order passed by the learned Sessions Judge under section 439A of the Code. It is to be seen whether the petitioner invokes the Court's revisional jurisdiction under the garb of an application under section 561A of the Code. If the condition of section 561A of the CrPC is fulfilled namely, "to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under this Code, or to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice" this Court may exercise its power under section 561A. In the case of professor Md. Shahabul Huda Vs Md. Shaji reported in BCR 1984 (AD) 468 the Appellate Division affirmed the order passed by the High Court Division in exercise of its jurisdiction under section 561 A against an order passed by the Sessions Judge under section 439A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and it was observed"……………..There is no legal provision which empowers a Magistrate under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, to physically oust a person in possession of the disputed premises, during the pendency of such proceeding. In the facts and circumstances there is no illegality in quashing the proceedings drawn upon under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in exercise of jurisdiction under section 561A of the said Code as the proceeding amounts to abuse of the process of the Court." In the instant case we have clearly found that the learned Magistrate passed the order for custody of the petitioner aged above 16 years and for allowing her father to take her custody against her will. The girl has already expressed her opinion against giving her in custody of her father and she also filed an application to set her free. The learned Sessions Judge misconstrued the provisions of Bangladesh Majority Act which have no manner of application to the present case, Age limit of 18 years is mentioned for the purpose of marriage only in Child Marriage Restraint Act. A person cannot be treated as major under the Bangladesh Majority Act unless he or she attains the age of 18 years. This provision has nothing to do with the present case but it has been made for other purpose namely, for the purpose of entering into contracts with others, etc. Of course a District Court within the meaning of the Guardians and Wards Act may appoint a guardian for the person who has not attained the age of 18 years in appropriate cases for the welfare of such minors if the conditions laid down in that Act are fulfilled. The Sessions Judge therefore misapplied the provisions of the aforesaid Acts and acted illegally in affirming the unauthorised order passed by the learned Magistrate. 

 14. In the facts and circumstances as discussed above, we are of the opinion that the impugned orders are nullity and are abuse of process of the Court and our interference under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is necessary to prevent the abuse of the process of the Court in order to secure the ends of justice.
